items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we wish to evaluate the expression [MATH: \sqrt x + 3] for the value [MATH: x=9.] This type of expression is called a radical expression because it contains the radical symbol [MATH: \sqrt{\phantom 0}.] Remember that [MATH: \sqrt x] means "the positive square root of the number [MATH: x.]"

Content:
To evaluate this expression at the given value, we replace [MATH: x] with [MATH: 9] in the given expression and simplify.

Content:
[MATH: sqrt(x) + 3|=; sqrt(9) + 3|=; sqrt(3^{2}) + 3|=; 3 + 3|=; 6]

Content:
Important: You may have heard somewhere that [MATH: \sqrt{9} = \pm 3,] because [MATH: (-3)^2=9] and [MATH: (3)^2 = 9.] However, when we write down [MATH: \sqrt{9},] we always mean "the positive square root of [MATH: 9]".

Content:
If we want the negative square root of [MATH: 9], we write [MATH: -\sqrt{9} = -3.] Sometimes, we want both, in which case we would write [MATH: \pm\sqrt{9}=\pm 3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Content:
To evaluate this expression at the given value, we replace [MATH: x] with [MATH: 9] in the given expression and simplify.

Content:
[MATH: sqrt(x) + 3|=; sqrt(9) + 3|=; sqrt(3^{2}) + 3|=; 3 + 3|=; 6]

Content:
Important: You may have heard somewhere that [MATH: \sqrt{9} = \pm 3,] because [MATH: (-3)^2=9] and [MATH: (3)^2 = 9.] However, when we write down [MATH: \sqrt{9},] we always mean "the positive square root of [MATH: 9]".

Content:
